## Simon Willison from Simon Willison’s Newsletter — Running Python code in a sandbox with MicroPython and WASM

_From: `[email]` · 2026-06-06T04:45:02+00:00_

View this post on the web at https://simonw.substack.com/p/running-python-code-in-a-sandbox

In this newsletter:
Running Python code in a sandbox with MicroPython and WASM
Plus 7 links and 4 quotations and 2 notes and 6 releases and 1 research report and 2 tools
Sponsor message: AWS Summit NYC returns June 17 with 200+ expert lead sessions covering AI, cloud infrastructure, and security. Developers, architects, and tech leaders can explore hands-on workshops, live demos, and real-world implementation insights. If you’re building or scaling your systems, this free, in-person event is for you. Register here [ https://substack.com/redirect/7e31717a-6f86-458b-b61a-5983b4cacad1?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ].
Running Python code in a sandbox with MicroPython and WASM [ https://substack.com/redirect/1ff76a64-a253-4ce9-99c0-fe42d7091096?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] - 2026-06-06
I’ve been experimenting with different approaches to running code in a sandbox for several years now, but my latest attempt feels like it might finally have all of the characteristics I’ve been looking for. I’ve released it as an alpha package called micropython-wasm [ https://substack.com/redirect/9a097f49-efd0-4f0a-8af6-9ba9c01fe612?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ], and I’m using it for a code execution sandbox plugin for Datasette Agent [ https://substack.com/redirect/ded85f81-61d8-4eab-87fc-6bd2bec21f38?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] called datasette-agent-micropython [ https://substack.com/redirect/4e21c751-670a-46f5-9490-60c1891fec7f?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ].
Why do I want a sandbox? [ https://substack.com/redirect/75db7b61-61a8-4322-a379-7d8725442a4d?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]
What I want from a sandbox [ https://substack.com/redirect/929cab87-5368-4423-9ff8-c2f22107dd05?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]
WebAssembly looks really promising here [ https://substack.com/redirect/e1f31493-6db9-4d5a-96d3-c539213dccfd?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]
MicroPython in WebAssembly [ https://substack.com/redirect/37e6062a-4de4-4d24-80d3-39239f74e046?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]
Building the first version [ https://substack.com/redirect/1c3a2f4a-50a7-4cda-b169-ac18f6825308?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]
Try it yourself [ https://substack.com/redirect/6b1d697d-120f-4bc8-8fd3-de4e7f0b5568?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]
Should you trust my vibe-coded sandbox? [ https://substack.com/redirect/d01e518e-30fe-447b-bcc9-f0fa4d9e759a?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]
Why do I want a sandbox?
My key open source projects - Datasette [ https://substack.com/redirect/f6ffba15-ac66-4249-8b51-0fba43618557?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ], LLM [ https://substack.com/redirect/7a5edffb-db31-419d-9888-88572eaec194?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ], even sqlite-utils [ https://substack.com/redirect/378fe1bb-1cf3-43e1-89d9-9baeb55909cd?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] - all support plugins.
I absolutely love plugins as a mechanism for extending software. A carefully designed plugin system reduces the risk involved in trying new things to almost nothing - even the wildest ideas won’t leave a lasting influence on the core application itself. My software can grow a new feature overnight and I don’t even have to review a pull request!
There’s one major drawback: my plugin systems all use Python and Pluggy [ https://substack.com/redirect/50c2fb99-3dbd-4db9-8e44-00aa0a6c6328?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ], and plugin code executes with full privileges within my applications. A buggy or malicious plugin could break everything or leak private data.
I’d love to be able to run plugin-style code in an environment where it is unable to read unapproved files, connect to a network, or generally operate in a way that’s risky or harmful to the rest of the application or the user’s computer.
My interest covers more than just plugins. For Datasette in particular there are many features I’d like to support where arbitrary code execution would be useful. I’ve already experimented with this for Datasette Enrichments [ https://substack.com/redirect/a56a14a7-1b0b-4e4b-bd6e-a8db741b61b9?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ], where code can be used to transform values stored in a table. I’d love to build a mechanism where you can run code on a schedule that fetches JSON from an approved location, runs a tiny bit of code to reformat it into a list of dictionaries, then inserts those as rows in a SQLite database table.
What I want from a sandbox
My goal is to execute code safely within my own Python applications. Here’s what I need:
Dependencies that cleanly install from PyPI, including binary wheels across multiple platforms if necessary. I don’t want people using my software to have to take any extra steps beyond directly installing my Python package.
Executed code must be subject to both memory and CPU limits. I don’t want while True: s += "longer string" to crash my application or the user’s computer.
File access must be strictly controlled. Either no filesystem access at all or I get to define exactly which files can be read and which files can be written to.
Network access is controlled as well. Sandboxed code should not be able to communicate with anything without going through a layer I fully control.
Support for interaction with host functions. A sandbox isn’t much use if I can’t carefully expose selected platform features to the code that it’s running.
It has to be robust, supported, and clearly documented. I’ve lost count of the number of sandbox projects I’ve seen in repos with warnings that they aren’t actively maintained!
WebAssembly looks really promising here
Web browsers operate in the most hostile environment imaginable when it comes to malicious code. Their job is to download and execute untrusted code from the web on almost every page load.
Given this, JavaScript engines should be excellent candidates for sandboxes. Sadly those engines are also extremely complicated, and are not designed for easy embedding in other projects. Most of the v8-in-Python projects I’ve seen are infrequently maintained and come with warnings not to use them with completely untrusted code.
WebAssembly is a much better candidate. It was designed from the start to support all of the characteristics I care about and has been tested in browsers for nearly a decade. The wasmtime [ https://substack.com/redirect/bb709941-a419-4fad-956c-b26f7c56ab0d?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] Python library is actively maintained and has binary wheels.
MicroPython in WebAssembly
WebAssembly engines like wasmtime run WebAssembly binaries. Some programming languages like Rust are easy to compile directly to WebAssembly. Dynamic languages like JavaScript and Python are harder - they support language primitives like eval(), which means they need a full interpreter available at runtime.
To run Python we need a full Python interpreter compiled to WebAssembly, wired up in a way that makes it easy to feed it code, hook up host functions and access the results.
Pyodide offers an outstanding package for running Python using WebAssembly in the browser, but using Pyodide in server-side Python isn’t supported. The most recent advice I could find was from October 2024 [ https://substack.com/redirect/3ff84589-4207-41e3-813a-678ee58797d2?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1

 [LEARN MORE] 
 2. WHAT DO YOUR CONVERSIONS MEAN? 
 The biggest mistake you're likely to make is to take your conversion results at face value. There are specific steps you can take to both understand what results mean and act on that information. You can also uncover new data that isn't disclosed by default.

 A couple of months ago, advertisers on LinkedIn were raving about a new feature called Customer Lifecycle Strategy.  While I'm cautiously pro-AI, I'm not fanatical about it. I worry about the very real risks involved. And when it comes to managing your ads, it's important to understand where the greatest risks and opportunities are. It's the focus of this week's Pubcast Question (4 minutes).

## Startup Spells — 🪄 NASA-grade marketing for $2 drinks

_From: `[email]` · 2026-06-06T14:06:34+00:00_

Red Bull turned extreme stunts into marketing that earns more coverage than any ad buy ever could. The company doesn't interrupt your entertainment. It builds the entertainment from scratch, slaps its logo on it, and lets the cameras roll.

Think of a bar that throws the best parties in town. Nobody goes there because of the drink menu. They go because something is always happening. Red Bull figured this out before most tech companies did.

The best example is still the one that nearly broke YouTube.

## 128,100 Feet Above Earth, Dressed in Red Bull Logos

On October 14, 2012, Felix Baumgartner stepped off a capsule 128,100 feet above New Mexico. He was wearing a pressurized suit covered in Red Bull logos. Below him: the entire curvature of the Earth.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/d35c19b2-28ee-4611-be71-9869038bea26/red-bull-extreme-stunts-marketing-strategy.jpg?t=1780731971)
Caption: Red Bull extreme stunts marketing Felix Baumgartner stepping off Stratos capsule at 128,100 feet

Felix hit [1,357 km/h](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Bull_Stratos) in freefall. Mach 1.24. He became the first human to break the sound barrier without a vehicle. The freefall lasted about 4 minutes and 20 seconds before he deployed his parachute. Total descent: [10 minutes](https://www.redbull.com/int-en/projects/red-bull-stratos).

The broadcast numbers were absurd. Over [8 million people watched simultaneously on YouTube](https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaelhumphrey/2012/10/14/red-bull-stratos-live-topped-8-million-concurrent-views-on-youtube/), a record at the time. The stream ran across [40+ TV networks in 50 countries](https://www.marketingweek.com/red-bull-brand-boosted-by-space-skydive/).

Twitter logged over 3 million tweets during the event. Over the years, the footage has piled up [close to a billion views](https://www.redbull.com/us-en/felix-baumgartner-stratos-10-years).

All of it for an energy drink company. Most companies [rent attention](https://startupspells.com/p/puma-120k-pele-deal-1970-world-cup) by buying ad slots. Red Bull built its own stadium and sold out every seat.

## Real Scientists, Real Data, Real Cameras

Most branded stunts are filmed in a day. Stratos was a [5-year engineering project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Bull_Stratos).

Red Bull worked with scientists, engineers, and medical researchers. The project generated real data for high-altitude escape systems and [spaceflight safety research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Bull_Stratos).

Felix completed multiple [test jumps months before the final attempt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Bull_Stratos). This was not a publicity team winging it. It was closer to an actual space program.

The production looked like it too. Dozens of cameras covered the capsule, the suit, and the ground setup. Live telemetry and biometric monitoring ran throughout.

A real-time mission control broadcast went out to the world. It looked like [NASA](https://digitalsynopsis.com/advertising/red-bull-stratos-felix-baumgartner-space-jump/), not advertising.

The distribution was designed from the start for global reach. The livestream was [embedded across multiple platforms](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Bull_Stratos), not just YouTube. Broadcast hit TV and digital simultaneously.

Social media was woven into the experience with live questions and reactions from viewers.

The whole thing was [built as a campaign study](https://scoreindia.org/blog/campaign-case-study-red-bull-stratos-experiential-marketing/) in how to make marketing that people actually want to watch.

## The Events Red Bull Manufactures on Repeat

Stratos was not a one-off. Red Bull manufactures events across different formats, all following the same principle: build something so wild that [the media covers it for free](https://startupspells.com/p/marketing-mschf-emotion-first-playbook-behind-viral-hits).

Here are 3 formats that prove the pattern holds.

### Flugtag

Teams build homemade flying machines out of whatever they can find and launch them off a pier into water. The machines almost never fly. That is the entire point.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/1fce80fe-3809-43fa-a432-85b7bae90091/red-bull-flugtag-flying-machine-pier.jpg?t=1780731991)
Caption: Red Bull Flugtag homemade flying machine launching off pier

The events run globally across Europe, the US, and Asia. They are designed to be chaotic, funny, and extremely shareable.

Nobody watches Flugtag for the engineering. They watch it because a team dressed as cows just drove a cardboard biplane off a 30-foot platform.

### Near-Vertical Cliffs, Viral Every Year

Red Bull Rampage sends mountain bikers down near-vertical cliffs in the Utah desert. The riders carve their own lines into the rock. The event is known for crashes, massive drops, and clips that go viral every single year.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/aed1a671-5a26-4521-b2ec-6611cf416d2b/red-bull-rampage-cliff-jump-utah.jpg?t=1780732019)
Caption: Red Bull Rampage mountain biker jumping off cliff in Utah desert

It is considered one of the most dangerous mountain biking competitions in the world. And Red Bull owns every second of the footage.

Imagine owning the gym where every viral workout clip gets filmed. You do not need to post anything yourself. [Every athlete who walks in](https://startupspells.com/p/strava-sponsored-challenges-mobilize-50m-athletes-with-native-ads) becomes your marketing department.

### Air Race

Red Bull Air Race put pilots in small planes flying at roughly 370 km/h through inflatable pylons. Precision flying meets time trials, hosted in cities around the world.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/2d0b23b6-c70f-4b8d-9bde-b06938dbc239/red-bull-air-race-plane-helipad.jpg?t=1780732037)
Caption: Red Bull Air Race plane flying near helipad over water

The races turned skylines in Abu Dhabi, Budapest, and Las Vegas into racetracks. Every frame was content.

## The Franchise Model for Spectacle

[Red Bull GmbH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Bull_GmbH) is headquartered in Austria. It operates in over 170 countries. Each country has a local team that runs events regionally.

The system works like this: a central team creates the core format. Each country adapts it with local athletes, local audiences, and local culture.

Red Bull Batalla in Mexico means Spanish rap battles. Batalla in India means Hindi and English. Same structure. Different flavor.

It is like a franchise restaurant. The menu is the same everywhere, but the spice levels adjust to the local palate.

Not every event runs everywhere. Rampage only happens in Utah because the terrain demands it. Flugtag and Soapbox Race can run in any major city with a waterfront or a hill. Cliff Diving rotates through coastal stops globally.

At any given point in the year, [Red Bull has](https://www.redbull.com/int-en/events/) a dance event running in India, a cliff diving stop somewhere in Europe, a motorsport event in the Middle East, and a flagship stunt in the US. All at the same time.

In a typical year, the calendar looks something like this: 1 Rampage in Utah, 6 Cliff Diving stops across Europe, 10+ countries hosting Batalla qualifiers, 5 to 10 cities running Soapbox or Flugtag.

Add a handful of dance and drift events scattered across Asia and the Middle East.

Red Bull did not just run one big stunt and call it a strategy. They built a machine that runs dozens of events across continents, [all year, every year](https://startupspells.com/p/oreo-marketing-playboo
